1. Begin each morning by telling yourself: today I shall meet people who are meddling, ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, and careless of others. They are like this because they do not know what is good and what is bad. But I have seen what the good is, and that it is noble; and what the bad is, and that it is shameful. And I have seen what the wrongdoer himself is: he is my kin—not only because we share the same blood or seed, but because we share the same intelligence and the same portion of the divine. So none of them can harm me, since none of them can drag me into anything shameful. Nor can I be angry with my kinsman or hate him. For we were made to work together, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the upper and lower rows of teeth. To work against one another, then, is against nature; and to resent someone and turn away from him is to work against him.

2. Whatever this is that I am, it is a little flesh, a little breath, and the ruling faculty—the reasoning mind that governs the rest of me. Throw away your books; stop letting yourself be distracted; that is no longer allowed. Instead, as though you were already dying, think nothing of the flesh: it is blood and bones and a network, a woven tangle of nerves, veins and arteries. Look at the breath too, and see what it is: air, and never the same air, but every moment breathed out and drawn in again. The third part, then, is the ruling faculty. Consider this: you are an old man, so do not let this part be a slave any longer. Do not let it be jerked on strings like a puppet by impulses that set you against others. Do not let it be discontented any longer with what you have been given now, or shrink from what is to come.

3. Everything that comes from the gods is full of providence—the gods' care and foresight. Even what comes from fortune is not separate from nature; it is woven and bound together with the things that providence directs. Everything flows from providence. Necessity plays its part too, and so does what benefits the whole universe, of which you are a part. Whatever the nature of the universe brings about, and whatever keeps that nature in being, is good for every part of nature. And the universe is kept in being by change: by the changes of the elements, and equally by the changes of the things made from the elements. Let these principles be enough for you; hold them always as settled judgments. But throw away your thirst for books, so that you do not die grumbling, but cheerfully, sincerely, and grateful to the gods from your heart.

4. Remember how long you have been putting all this off, and how many times the gods have given you an opportunity that you have not used. It is time now, at last, to understand what universe you are a part of, and who governs that universe—the one from whom your own existence flows. Understand, too, that a limit has been set to your time. If you do not use it to clear the clouds from your mind, it will pass, and you will pass, and it will never come back.

5. Every moment, set your mind firmly, as a Roman and a man, on doing the task in front of you with complete and unpretentious dignity, with warmth, freedom and justice. And set it on freeing yourself from every other thought. You will free yourself if you do each act of your life as if it were your last: without carelessness, without the passionate aversion that turns away from what reason commands, without pretense, without self-love, and without discontent with the share you have been given. You see how few things there are: whoever holds on to them is able to live a life that flows quietly, like the life of the gods. For the gods, on their part, will ask nothing more of someone who keeps to these things.

6. Go on, keep wronging yourself, my soul, keep wronging yourself! But you will no longer have the chance to honor yourself. Each person's life is enough; but yours is nearly over, and still you do not respect yourself, but make your happiness depend on the souls of others.

7. Do the things that happen to you from outside distract you? Then give yourself time to learn something new and good, and stop being spun around. But you must also guard against being carried off in the other direction. For some people wear themselves out with activity all their lives, yet have no goal toward which to direct every impulse and, in short, every thought; and they too are wasting their lives on trifles.
8. People are seldom made unhappy by failing to notice what goes on in someone else's mind; but those who do not pay attention to the movements of their own minds are bound to be unhappy.

9. Always keep this in mind: what the nature of the whole is, and what my own nature is; how the one is related to the other; and what kind of part mine is, and of what kind of whole. And remember that no one can stop you from always doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which you are a part.

10. Theophrastus, comparing wrong acts as one would compare them by ordinary human standards, says, like a true philosopher, that wrongs done out of desire deserve more blame than wrongs done out of anger. For someone who is gripped by anger seems to turn away from reason with a kind of pain, and a shrinking inside that he is not aware of. But someone who does wrong out of desire, overcome by pleasure, seems in a way more self-indulgent and more womanish in his wrongdoing. So he was right, and spoke as a philosopher should, when he said that a wrong done with pleasure deserves more blame than one done with pain. In general, the angry person is more like someone who has first been wronged and is driven to anger by the pain of it; the other has set out to do wrong on his own impulse, carried into the act by desire.

11. Since you may leave life at any moment, let that thought govern everything you do and think. If there are gods, leaving the company of human beings is nothing to fear, for the gods would not involve you in anything bad. And if there are no gods, or if they do not care about human affairs, why should I want to live in a universe without gods, or without providence? But in fact they do exist, and they do care about human affairs, and they have put it entirely in a person's power not to fall into what is truly bad. As for everything else, if any of it were bad, they would have provided for that too, so that it would be entirely in a person's power not to fall into it. And how can something that does not make a person worse make that person's life worse? If such things were bad, the nature of the universe could not have let them slip past it—not from ignorance, and not from knowing about them but lacking the power to prevent or correct them. Nor could it have made so great a mistake, through lack of power or lack of skill, that good and bad things would fall without distinction on good people and bad. Yet death and life, honor and dishonor, pain and pleasure all happen equally to good people and bad, and they make us neither better nor worse. Therefore they are neither good nor bad.

12. How quickly everything vanishes: the bodies themselves vanish into the universe, and even the memory of them vanishes into time. Consider what all the things the senses perceive really are—especially those that lure us with the bait of pleasure, or frighten us with pain, or are made famous by empty reputation—how worthless, contemptible, dirty, perishable and dead they are. It is the work of our power of understanding to observe this. It should observe, too, who these people are whose opinions and voices make a reputation. And it should observe what death is: if a person looks at death by itself, and by the power of thought takes apart everything the imagination has attached to it, he will see that it is nothing but a process of nature; and anyone who is afraid of a process of nature is a child. Yet death is not only a process of nature; it also serves nature's purposes. And it should observe how a human being comes near to God, through what part of himself he does so, and in what condition that part is when he does.

13. Nothing is more wretched than a person who runs around in circles after everything, and pries into the things beneath the earth, as the poet says, and tries to guess what is going on in his neighbors' minds, without realizing that it is enough to attend to the divine spirit within him—the guiding mind that is his share of the divine—and to honor it sincerely. And honoring it means keeping it pure from passion, from thoughtlessness, and from discontent with what comes from gods and human beings. For what comes from the gods deserves reverence because of its excellence. What comes from human beings should be dear to us because we are kin; and sometimes, in a way, it even moves our pity, because people do not know good from bad—a blindness no less serious than the one that leaves us unable to tell white from black.

14. Even if you were going to live three thousand years, or ten thousand times that, still remember that no one loses any life except the one he is living now, and no one lives any life except the one he is losing. So the longest life and the shortest come to the same thing. For the present moment is the same for everyone, even though the time that has passed away is not the same for all; and so what is lost turns out to be a mere moment. No one can lose the past or the future: how could anyone take from a person what he does not have? So you must keep these two things in mind. First, that all things have had the same forms from eternity and come round again in a circle, and that it makes no difference whether a person watches the same things for a hundred years, or two hundred, or for endless time. Second, that the person who lives longest and the person who dies soonest lose exactly the same. For the present is the only thing anyone can be deprived of—if it is true that it is the only thing he has, and that no one can lose what he does not have.

15. Remember that everything is opinion—what we judge things to be. For what the Cynic Monimus said is plain; and plain too is how useful his saying is, if you take from it what it has to offer, as far as it is true.

16. The human soul does violence to itself, first of all, when it becomes, as far as it can, an abscess, a kind of tumor on the universe. For to resent anything that happens is to break away from nature, which holds within it, each in its part, the natures of all other things. Second, the soul does violence to itself when it turns away from another person, or even goes at him meaning to harm him, as the souls of angry people do. Third, when it is overcome by pleasure or by pain. Fourth, when it puts on an act, and does or says anything falsely or insincerely. Fifth, when it lets any act or impulse of its own go without an aim, and does anything thoughtlessly, without considering what it is doing. For even the smallest things ought to be done for a purpose; and the purpose of rational beings is to follow the reason and the law of the oldest city and commonwealth of all—the universe itself.

17. In human life, time is a point; the stuff we are made of is always flowing; our perception is dim; the whole body, as it is put together, is prone to rot; the soul is a whirl; fortune is hard to predict; and fame has no judgment. In a word, everything belonging to the body is a river, and everything belonging to the soul is a dream and a vapor; life is a war and a stay in a foreign land; and after fame comes oblivion. What, then, can guide a person through it? One thing, and only one: philosophy. And philosophy means keeping the divine spirit within a person safe from violence and harm, stronger than pains and pleasures; doing nothing without a purpose, and nothing falsely or hypocritically; not needing anyone else to do or not do anything; accepting everything that happens and everything that is given to him as coming from the same source he himself came from, wherever that source may be; and, finally, waiting for death with a cheerful mind, since death is nothing but the breaking up of the elements that every living being is made of. And if the elements themselves come to no harm in constantly changing into one another, why should anyone fear the change and breaking up of all of them? It is in keeping with nature, and nothing that is in keeping with nature is bad. Written at Carnuntum.
